Esau was the elder twin son of Isaac and grandson of Abraham who lost both his birthright and his blessing to his twin brother Jacob through cunning and hunger. He was born first and thus initially the rightful heir to Isaac's estate and the covenant with God; his name means red in Hebrew. Esau was a skilled hunter and man of the field, contrasting with Jacob's tent-dwelling, shepherding character. This dichotomy highlights competing modes of existence and spiritual priorities. He sold his birthright to Jacob for a bowl of lentils when he returned famished from hunting, establishing the pattern of spiritual compromise for immediate gratification. Later, when Jacob, disguised in sheepskin and goat hair, deceived their dying father Isaac into bestowing the patriarchal blessing on him instead, Esau wept in anguish. He fled in humiliation and lived in the region of Seir, where his descendants became known as Edomites, a perennial foe of Israel. Despite the deception, Esau later reconciled with Jacob after Jacob's long exile; the brothers met, embraced, and wept together in reconciliation, subverting the narrative's earlier tone of rivalry. The biblical narrative frames him as the one rejected in favor of Jacob despite being firstborn, illustrating divine election based on spiritual rather than natural right.
